metadata.title: Driving a World from an App

inlineContent.text: A world is a value, and a schedule changes it through an
parameter. The code that drives
it, such as a game engine’s frame callback or an app’s model object, owns the world, runs a
schedule on it, and reads the results. This article shows how to pass input in, how to hold the
world, and how objects outside the world can take part in a step while a schedule runs.

content.text: Pass Each Run’s Input Through a Resource

inlineContent.text: A system’s
method receives only the world, so input that changes from run to
run, such as the time since the last frame or the buttons held down, goes into a resource before
each run. Systems read it with a
like any other resource:

code: func run(_ movers: Update<Position>.Over<Velocity>, _ step: ResourceReader<TimeStep>) {
let ball = world.spawn(Position(x: 0, y: 0), Velocity(dx: 2, dy: 0))

inlineContent.text: Inserting a resource replaces the one of the same type, so the schedule stays the same from frame
to frame; there is no need to rebuild it, or to store the input in a system. A system’s declared
access lists the resource like any other, so a schedule still knows which systems can run at the
same time.

content.text: Hold the World in a Final Class

inlineContent.text: An app’s model object or an engine’s node usually owns the world. Store it in a stored
property of a
class, and run schedules on that property:

code: let rocket = game.world.spawn(Position(x: 0, y: 0), Velocity(dx: 0, dy: 4))

inlineContent.text: Reading through a stored property, as
does, reads the
world in place. A getter that returns a world, such as a computed property or a protocol
requirement the compiler can’t see through, returns a copy instead. A copy shares the world’s
storage rather than duplicating it, but it costs more than reading in place on every access; in a
loop that reads many values, read through the stored property or pass the world down as shown
next.

content.text: Let Outside Objects Take Part in a Step

inlineContent.text: While a schedule runs, it has exclusive access to the world it was given. An object that reaches
back to the property holding the world during the run, such as a view that reads
from inside a system, overlaps that access, and Swift stops the program with an exclusivity
violation.
Instead, pass the world to the object. Give it a method that takes the world as an
parameter, and call that method from a
that holds the object:

code: let ship = world.spawn(Position(x: 0, y: 0), Velocity(dx: 3, dy: 0))

inlineContent.text: The object reads and writes the world it is handed, and the schedule orders its work with the
other systems like any other system’s. A main-actor system runs on the main actor, so it can call
into views and other objects isolated to it.

content.text: Perform Effects Before a Step Continues

inlineContent.text: Events suit effects the outside handles later: a system sends them, and the outside reads them
after the schedule runs. Some effects have to happen before the step goes on, such as a message
the view must show before the next system changes what it describes. A main-actor system calls
the object directly, and the call returns before the next system in the schedule starts:

code: for (_, health) in world.query(Health.self) where health.current <= 0 {

inlineContent.text: When the outside needs more than one call to respond, such as an animation that must finish
first, end the step there: split the work into two schedules, run the first, and run the second
when the outside reports that it is done.
